title: Before we begin…
message: Three quick questions. A show of hands is enough.
body: Do you have a ChatGPT account (or Gemini, or Claude)?
Do you already use GenAI to study or prepare teaching materials?

title: Andrea needs to understand GenAI
message: One student’s learning process, from assignment to assessment
body: Andrea is a second-year computer science student: he can program, but still confuses key concepts of generative models.
He must study a chapter and explain how a language model generates text.
We observe his use of tools and the evidence of understanding he keeps.
decision: You are following the learning method; you do not need to learn programming.

title: The assigned book
message: Marco Cremaschi · Foundations of Generative Artificial Intelligence
body: Topic: Language Models and Basic Architecture.
The book is available as a PDF.

title: Andrea’s learning task
message: To understand the chapter and show what he has learned, Andrea must:

steps.title: Read
steps.text: Study the chapter. Identify the key ideas and what is still unclear.

steps.title: Represent
steps.text: Build a diagram with labelled links between the concepts.

steps.title: Check
steps.text: Compare the diagram and AI suggestions with the chapter. Correct errors.

steps.title: Explain
steps.text: Use his own words to explain a new example, without AI help.

decision: Evidence: a checked diagram, an independent explanation and a justified correction.

title: Self-directed learning: making choices
message: Andrea takes an active role: he identifies his learning needs, chooses a path and reviews his progress.

steps.title: Identify a goal
steps.text: What do I need to learn, and what do I want to achieve?

steps.title: Choose a path
steps.text: Which resources, people and strategies will help me learn?

steps.title: Review progress
steps.text: What can I explain now, and what needs more work? Self-assessment helps here.

result: “I need to distinguish training from inference. I will use the chapter and a concept map, then check whether I can explain the difference.”
decision: Andrea takes responsibility for his choices, with support from teachers and peers.

title: Self-assessment: checking progress
message: Andrea judges his progress against clear criteria, then uses that judgement to improve his work.

steps.title: Check the criteria
steps.text: What should I be able to explain or do?

steps.title: Look for evidence
steps.text: What can I demonstrate? Where do I still struggle?

steps.title: Choose a next step
steps.text: What will I revise, practise or check again?

result: “I can explain the main ideas, but I still struggle to show how they connect. I will revise my map and explain those connections again.”
decision: AI can offer feedback; the learner checks the evidence and decides what to improve.

title: Why the learning design matters
message: Research informs how we design support and check understanding.

comparison.label: AI-assisted practice
comparison.text: In one high-school maths experiment, unguarded AI improved practice scores but reduced later unaided performance.

comparison.label: Self-assessment and revision
comparison.text: Learners use criteria and feedback to identify gaps and revise their work.

result: Check an independent explanation, use clear criteria and allow another attempt.
decision: Consider the study context when transferring these findings to another subject or age group.

title: A study process in six phases

steps.title: PLAN
steps.text: Set your goal, identify your starting point and organise tasks and time.

steps.title: UNDERSTAND
steps.text: Clarify difficult ideas through explanations, examples and questions.

steps.title: CONNECT
steps.text: Explain ideas in your own words and organise relationships between concepts.

steps.title: RECALL
steps.text: Retrieve what you know without looking, then revisit it over time.

steps.title: APPLY
steps.text: Use what you have learned to solve problems and handle new situations.

steps.title: CHECK
steps.text: Compare your performance with criteria, identify gaps and decide what to study next.

decision: Checking guides your next step. SUPPORT marks setup, sources and sharing.

title: My learning route
message: Andrea chooses his next step and keeps evidence of understanding.

steps.title: My goal
steps.text: Explain training, inference and RAG in my own words.

steps.title: My starting point
steps.text: I know the terms, but still confuse context with parameters.

steps.title: My next action
steps.text: Read sections 1.2 and 1.7, then build a map and check its links.

steps.title: My evidence
steps.text: With the chat closed, explain a new example in my own words.

steps.title: My next decision
steps.text: Revise one link, try another example or ask for a hint.

decision: At each checkpoint: how am I feeling, how confident am I, and what evidence supports that confidence?

title: Feelings, confidence and the next step
message: A short check-in helps Andrea choose the support he needs.

comparison.label: “I feel overwhelmed.”
comparison.text: Choose one small action. Ask for a hint, an example or teacher support.

comparison.label: “I am unsure.”
comparison.text: Name the exact point of uncertainty. Compare the explanation with the chapter.

comparison.label: “I feel very confident.”
comparison.text: Close the answer. Explain the idea and try a new example.

result: Choose one support and explain why it fits the current difficulty.
decision: The check-in can stay private. Feelings guide support; evidence guides judgements of understanding.

comparison.label: More control
comparison.text: Adapt explanations, questions and outputs to your learning goal.

comparison.label: A connected workflow
comparison.text: Use the same materials across different study activities.

comparison.label: Transferable skills
comparison.text: Reuse the method across subjects and AI assistants.

comparison.label: Potential savings
comparison.text: Cover several needs before paying for additional tools.

title: What can ChatGPT do?
message: Turn a topic into materials for understanding, practice and revision.

comparison.label: Informal · prompt label

decision: A prompt label guides the response; it does not guarantee an interactive result.

title: Five risks, five classroom checks
message: Choose a safeguard for the activity you are about to try.

comparison.label: Hallucination
comparison.text: Open the source and check whether it supports the exact claim.

comparison.label: Bias
comparison.text: Examine assumptions, stereotypes and perspectives missing from the answer.

comparison.label: Overconfidence
comparison.text: Compare confidence with an explanation produced independently.

comparison.label: Privacy
comparison.text: Use public or fictional examples. Keep identifiable student information out of prompts.

comparison.label: Over-reliance
comparison.text: Keep an initial attempt, use limited assistance and finish with an independent check.

decision: The teacher reviews content, access and safeguards. Which risk matters most in your activity?

title: Skills for studying the same chapter
message: Three reusable workflows, tested with Andrea’s assigned book.
decision: Choose a support for the next learning action, then check its output.

title: Learn: explain before receiving feedback
message: Andrea tests his understanding of training, inference and RAG.
prompt: I am Andrea, a second-year computer science student studying the attached workshop book, Foundations of Generative Artificial Intelligence. Help me understand training, ordinary inference and RAG using only §§1.2 and 1.7. I keep thinking that adding a definition to a prompt updates the weights. Start with one diagnostic question and wait for my answer. Keep each turn under 100 words and cite the chapter section. Answer in English.
decision: Explain what changed before reading the feedback.

title: Build a study kit after recall
message: The same chapter becomes practice materials and two short reviews.
prompt: I am Andrea, studying the attached workshop book, Foundations of Generative Artificial Intelligence. Use only §§1.2 and 1.7 to help me distinguish training, ordinary inference and RAG. My goal is to explain what changes without assistance. I have 10 minutes today and two 5-minute reviews this week. Start one short recall question and wait for my answer. Keep replies under 100 words. After the practice, make a compact source-linked study kit. Answer in English.
decision: Compare your explanation with the model answer, then assess it against the criteria.

title: Compare the chapter in an editable diagram
message: Training, ordinary inference and RAG retain distinct flows.
prompt: Using only §§1.2 and 1.7 of the attached workshop book, make a compact Mermaid flowchart that Andrea can edit. Compare training, ordinary inference and RAG, with labelled arrows showing what changes and what stays fixed. Include an accessible title and description, a short text alternative and chapter-section references. Limit the diagram to 10 nodes. Answer in English.
decision: Check each arrow against the chapter, then explain the diagram independently.

decision: Keep the useful steps; adjust detail where Andrea is stuck.

decision: Compare the suggested time window with the time Andrea actually needs.

title: Taskmaster: work on one task

title: Professor: request an explanation
message: Ask for a short explanation and example of training versus inference.
decision: Check parameter updates and the limits of the analogy against the assigned chapter.

title: Formalizer: revise the wording
message: Compare a student draft with the “More professional” rewrite.
decision: Check that the distinction and the student’s remaining uncertainty survive the rewrite.

title: Ask a focused question
message: Request a short explanation with references to the chapter
body: The need is to understand why an answer can change without retraining.
prompt: Using only the uploaded chapter, explain the difference between learned parameters and context during ordinary inference. Use three short points and cite the chapter. Then give one example involving a definition added to a prompt. Answer in English.
decision: Read the answer, then check whether each reference supports its claim.

title: Open the citation and its source
message: Compare the generated claim with the original passage

steps.title: Open the reference
steps.text: Select the citation for the statement about parameters.

steps.title: Read before and after
steps.text: Check conditions and meaning in the original paragraph.

steps.title: Compare the wording
steps.text: Does the answer retain “during inference”, or has it become “always”?

decision: Preserve the condition ‘during ordinary inference’ when reusing the explanation.

title: Set up a Learning Guide
message: Choose the conversation goal and response length

title: Check the analogy as well
message: A metaphor helps when its boundary remains visible
body: Back to the source: during ordinary inference, context enters the calculation and parameters are not updated.

comparison.label: A useful analogy
comparison.text: Context is like material available on a desk during a task.

comparison.label: A boundary to state
comparison.text: The model does not read as a person does; the analogy does not describe its internal calculation.

decision: Andrea should be able to express the concept without the metaphor.
